newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK election to be remembered as watershed.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK election to be remembered as watershed.

text.p: The British election, widely tipped in opinion polls to be won by the opposition Labour party, will go down in history as a major turning point in the country's politics, election experts said on Wednesday.
Almost half of 20 experts in a Reuters survey on the outcome of the May 1 election said it would be remembered as a watershed, turning around 18 years of Conservative rule.
"It will be remembered as the election that was as historically significant as the 1979 election," said Justin Fisher, lecturer in political science at London Guildhall University.
He said there would be a fundamental realignment of British voting habits, with large groups of former Conservative voters coming over to Labour and staying with them.
The panellists said the Labour party was on the threshold of an era of political domination which they had not enjoyed since 1964.

"The argument is that the pendulum of public opinion has swung back. There is an adjustment going on in terms of public support," said John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester. "People are moving away from conspicuous consumption and towards social cohesion and collective provisions."
The mean of 20 forecasts from the Reuters panel put the overall Labour majority at 82 seats, slightly up from 79 seats a week ago.
Nineteen of the 20 panellists expect Labour to win a majority in the election. David Carlton, lecturer in politics at the University of Warwick, predicts no overall majority for either party.
He believes the most memorable event of this election would be the extent to which the final results would prove opinion polls wrong.
"The panel is out of line with the opinion polls which are suggesting more than a 200-seat majority for Labour."
"Either the panel will have egg on their faces or the polls will. Even if we all say Labour is going to win, it's not good enough. The actual majority is also important," Carlton said.
Irreconcilable differences over plans for Europe's single currency was mentioned by five of the panellists who were asked how this election would be remembered.

Four of the panellists labelled this election campaign as boring and tedious. Three said collective memory would focus on allegations of sex and financial scandals and corruption against the Conservative government.
Ivor Crewe, vice-chancellor at the University of Essex, said this would be one of the more forgettable election campaigns of the century. But he noted that the result would be remembered.
"I don't think the campaign has come alive. No issue has been the subject of sustained debate and captured the public's imagination," said Crewe.
"The parties have been regarded as much of a muchness and public expectations about the capacity of either party to solve problems are low."
The last Reuters survey of expert opinion on the outcome of the election will be published on Wednesday April 30, the day before the country goes to the polls.
